title: Slow: The Birth of Slowcore (1989–2000)
author: Claudette
description: Codeine, Bedhead, Low & the sad underground that invented slowcore before it had a name. From Galaxie 500's quiet revolution to Duster's four-track basement — deep cuts only, 1989–2000.

nodes.name: Kramer (producer)
nodes.note: recorded Galaxie 500's Today (1988, 3 days, $750) AND produced Low's I Could Live in Hope (1994) — the genre's birth certificate in two sessions

nodes.name: Galaxie 500
nodes.note: Harvard trio — Wareham, Krukowski, Yang. Polyvinyl: 'a straight line from here to Low'

nodes.name: American Music Club
nodes.note: formed SF 1982 — Eitzel wrote the sadcore playbook before the word existed

nodes.name: Souled American
nodes.note: Chicago, 1986 — 'slowcore before that term existed' (their own bio); Tuma later joined Boxhead Ensemble

nodes.name: Codeine

nodes.name: Red House Painters
nodes.note: 4AD released their demo as Down Colorful Hill (1992); '24' = 'the magisterial slowcore opener' (Pitchfork)

nodes.name: Smog
nodes.note: Bill Callahan's first Drag City album, Julius Caesar (1993) — 4-track bedroom murk

nodes.name: Bedhead
nodes.note: Kadane brothers, Dallas — WhatFunLifeWas (1994) on King Coffey's Trance Syndicate, $3,000 budget

nodes.name: Low
nodes.note: Sparhawk & Parker, Duluth — I Could Live in Hope (1994, Vernon Yard, prod. Kramer); the band that made 'slowcore' a word

nodes.name: David Grubbs
nodes.note: Gastr del Sol — guest guitar on Codeine's The White Birch (tracks 'Tom' & 'Wird')

nodes.name: Vernon Yard
nodes.note: the label nexus — released Low's first three records; Acetone were its first-ever signing

nodes.name: Acetone
nodes.note: LA trio — 'LA's perfect forgotten band' (Sam Sweet); later on Neil Young's Vapor; Richie Lee died 2001

nodes.name: Mojave 3
nodes.note: ex-Slowdive's Halstead & Goswell rebuilding at half speed on 4AD (1995)

nodes.name: Dirty Three (Turner & White)

nodes.name: Cat Power
nodes.note: Moon Pix (1998) — written in one night after a nightmare, cut in Melbourne

nodes.name: Duster

nodes.name: Songs: Ohia / Jason Molina
nodes.note: the inheritor — The Lioness (2000), cut in Glasgow; Krassner (Boxhead, ex-Tuma orbit) produced Axxess & Ace

essay:
Some genres name themselves. Slowcore was named by everyone except the people playing it. It began as a critic's tag — 'sadcore,' then 'slowcore' — thrown at bands who answered the late-'80s loudness arms race by simply stopping. The joke hardened into a genre by the mid-'90s, largely on the back of one tiny label, Vernon Yard, while the bands themselves mostly hated the word. The music did the talking: songs that moved at the speed of weather fronts, guitars that rang and decayed like struck bells, drummers who treated the hi-hat as a luxury item. Slowness was never the point — gravity was. Codeine's Stephen Immerwahr said the songs weren't slow for effect; they were just heavy. The tempo was the weight settling.

The family tree is small and tangled. Kramer — the New York producer who ran Shimmy-Disc — recorded Galaxie 500's Today in three days for $750 in 1988, then produced Low's debut I Could Live in Hope in 1994: the genre's birth certificate in two sessions. Vernon Yard (a Virgin offshoot) put out Low's first three records and signed Acetone as its first-ever band; when the label went bankrupt, Acetone landed on Neil Young's Vapor Records. Codeine's The White Birch had David Grubbs of Gastr del Sol guesting on guitar, and its drummer Doug Scharin went on to June of 44. Souled American's guitarist Scott Tuma ended up in Michael Krassner's Boxhead Ensemble — the same Krassner who produced Songs: Ohia's Axxess & Ace — and Jim White, who drummed on Cat Power's Moon Pix, also played on Tuma's solo records. Six degrees of slowcore, all of it within arm's reach.

The playlist runs the arc: Galaxie 500's quiet revolution (1988) and American Music Club's pre-genre sad canon; ground zero with Codeine's Frigid Stars (1990) and Souled American's molasses country; the canon years — Red House Painters' demo-tape masterpiece Down Colorful Hill (1992), Smog's bedroom Drag City debut (1993), Bedhead's WhatFunLifeWas and Low's I Could Live in Hope (1994); then the second wave: Mojave 3's dream-pop crossover, Idaho's LA skeletalism, Acetone's lost LA masterpiece, Cat Power's nightmare-born Moon Pix, Duster's four-track Stratosphere — which Numero called the record that 'capped off and reinvented the slowcore's first wave' — closing on Jason Molina's Lioness, the heir apparent's benediction. Everything after is just the echo.
